status_summary: OMB's Director delegated apportionment authority to the Program Associate Directors effective 2025-02-11, superseding prior delegations (the notice lets them re-delegate in writing), and a successor notice effective 2025-04-18 lists career officials only as fallbacks when the responsible director is unavailable during a continuity event. OMB has since used apportionment, spending-plan conditions and rescission requests to control spending. It sent a 4.9 billion dollar rescission request in late August 2025 with too little time left in the fiscal year for the 45-day congressional review, and on 2025-09-26 the Supreme Court, on an interim basis, stayed a lower-court order requiring about 4 billion dollars of those funds to be obligated. On 2026-09-25 it sent a second such request, about 810 million dollars per American Action Forum (Senate Budget Committee Democrats describe it as nearly 1 billion dollars); GAO reaffirmed on 2026-09-29 that the Impoundment Control Act does not allow withholding funds past their expiration, and on 2026-09-30 Senate Republicans blocked a bill to bar the practice. GAO has found several Impoundment Control Act violations, and a district court ordered OMB to restore its public apportionment website.

timeline.event: OMB Director Vought delegates apportionment authority to the Program Associate Directors, effective this date (Federal Register notice published 2025-02-18).
OMB deactivates its public apportionment website; a 2025-03-29 letter from Vought says apportionments hold sensitive, predecisional information. GAO disagreed in writing on 2025-04-08.
GAO issues its second finding of an Impoundment Control Act violation in two months, concerning the Institute of Museum and Library Services (exact June date not confirmed; first of month used).
In CREW v. OMB, the D.D.C. rules that removing the apportionment database violated the law and orders it restored; the D.C. Circuit denies a stay in August and OMB resumes posting on 2025-08-15.

The administration sends Congress a rescission request of about 4.9 billion dollars in foreign aid with fewer than 45 days left in the fiscal year, the approach critics call a pocket rescission; the funds expire 2025-09-30.

The Supreme Court, 6-3 and on a preliminary basis, stays a district court order requiring the foreign aid to be obligated, finding the government likely to show the Impoundment Control Act bars the plaintiffs' suit; the Court says this is not a final merits ruling.
Nextgov reports an OMB update to its internal-controls circular that says GAO's views are not binding on the executive branch; GAO objected.

A second rescission request, about 810 million dollars in 11 accounts, is sent five days before fiscal year end; GAO says on 2026-09-29 that pocket rescissions are not allowed and the Senate blocks a bill to bar them on 2026-09-30.

title: OMB political appointees sign apportionments and use them to steer agency spending
uncertainties: No reporting was found that directly describes who signs individual FY2025 or FY2026 apportionments, so the PAD-signing point rests on the two Federal Register delegation notices. Figures differ by source for the 2026 request: American Action Forum and the Independent Institute give about 810 million dollars, while the Senate Budget Committee Democrats and a Hill headline say nearly 1 billion dollars. The Rescissions Act of 2025 (enacted 2025-07-24, per a search result) is context, not an apportionment action. The Peace Corps and NIH examples of spending-plan footnotes came from advocacy or secondhand sources and are not relied on. The GAO count of violations changed over time and was not updated to October 2026.
